Decided May 6,
Appeal from the decision of Administrative Law Judge Robert G. Holt, issued
January 9, 2014. That decision affirmed the civil penalty assessment of $101,540.80
imposed against Pensco Trust Company by the Field Manager, Shoshone Field Office,
Bureau of Land Management, for violation of the Archeological Resources Protection
Act of 1979.
Affirmed.
1. Archeological Resources Protection Act of 1979: Civil Penalty
Assessment: Appeal from Decision of Administrative Law Judge
Where Appellant has not provided any evidence for
consideration and has not established error by the Administrative
Law Judge, the decision of the Administrative Law Judge will be
affirmed.
APPEARANCES: Philip A. Brown, Esq., Gooding, Idaho, for Appellant.
OPINION BY CHAIRMAN JAMES L. BYRNES
Pursuant to 43 C.F.R. § 7.37, Pensco Trust Company, Appellant, filed on
February 10, 2014, in this Office a Notice of Appeal and a Request for a Stay of the
decision issued by Administrative Law Judge Robert G. Holt on January 9, 2014, in
Pensco Trust Company v. BLM, ARPA 2013-01 (2014). Judge Holt found in his
decision that Appellant violated the Archaeological Resources Protection Act of
(ARPA), 16 U.S.C. §§ 470aa-470mm (2006), and that the civil penalty of
$101,540.80, as assessed by the Field Manager, Shoshone Field Office, Bureau of
Land Management (BLM), Shoshone, Idaho, was a reasonable and appropriate
penalty for the violation. BLM alleged that Appellant erected a building and other
improvements on public land adjacent to Appellant's Dry Creek Ranch and that
during the unauthorized construction it bladed through an archaeological site on the
west side of the building. Pursuant to ARPA, BLM assessed a penalty of $101,540.80
47

for restoration of the site and the destruction of the archaeological resource. The
administrative record in the proceeding as well as the submissions of Appellant were
received and reviewed by this Board. By Order dated March 20, 2014, we denied the
Appellant's Request for a Stay.
In its Notice of Appeal, Appellant asserts that the "record does not support the
findings that agents of Pensco or independent contractors caused the alleged
damage." Appellant also asserts that the "record does not support the finding that
there was damage to and archaeological resource, the amount of the assessed value
by the BLM or who caused the damage." Appellant further contends that the
Administrative Law Judge erred when he held that deficiencies in the Notice of
Violation and Notice of Assessment did not bar BLM from assessing civil damages.
This is essentially the entirety of the Appellant's argument and presentation. Under
43 C.F.R. § 4.703, Appellant had 30 days from the date of filing its appeal to submit
briefing to support its contentions. For whatever reason it did not. Thus, we have
only vague and generalized allegations of error in the decision under appeal.
[1] To prevail in an appeal of a decision of an Administrative Law Judge,
Appellant must specify the errors alleged with particularity and support those
allegations with specific evidence. In re Jack Lee Harebon, 27 OHA 225, 228 (2004).
After an examination and careful consideration of the decision of the Administrative
Law Judge, the administrative record, and the submissions of the parties, this Board
sees no reason to disturb any portion of the Administrative Law Judge's ruling,
findings, or conclusions. Appellant has not identified any error in the Administrative
Law Judge's decision. We find that the Administrative Law Judge's findings of fact
are supported by the evidence in the record. Therefore, we adopt the findings and
analysis of the Administrative Law Judge into this Opinion. A copy of that decision is
attached to this Opinion. The instant appeal is hereby denied. Judge Holt's decision
in the civil penalty proceeding of Pensco Trust Company v. BLM, ARPA 2013-01,
(2014), is affirmed and adopted.

Before: Administrative Law Judge Robert G. Holt
I. Introduction
This matter is before me on a request for hearing filed by Pensco Trust Co.
("Pensco") pursuant to 43 C.F.R. § 7.15 (g). The Bureau of Land Management
("BLM") has assessed a civil penalty against Pensco for violation of the
Archaeological Resources Protection Act of 1979 ("ARPA"), 16 U.S.C §§ 470aa -
470mm (2006).
BLM has alleged that Pensco erected a building and other improvements on
public land adjacent to Pensco's Dry Creek Ranch and that during the unauthorized
construction it bladed through an archaeological site on the west side of the
building. BLM assessed a penalty of $101,540.80.
47 OHA 11

ARPA 2013-01
At the hearing, Pensco presented evidence that neither its trustee nor its
manager bladed or authorized others to blade the archaeological site. Nevertheless I
find that the evidence shows that only Pensco agents or its contractors had access to
the site and that they caused the damage to the site. Because Pensco had ultimate
control of the activities at the site, ARPA makes it responsible for the damages.
The following sections will first provide more background information, then
discuss the burden and standard of proof, and finally analyze why Pensco is liable.
II. Background
The Gooding County Planning and Zoning office first made BLM aware of a
house being built on public lands. Tr. 83:23-84:6. Further investigation showed that
a house was being constructed on BLM land lying north of property owned by
Pensco known as the Dry Creek Ranch. BLM Exs. 6, 7,and 10. The land is located
northwest of Gooding in south central Idaho. BLM concluded that Pensco was
responsible for the unauthorized construction because it held the grazing permit on
the BLM land and controlled the only vehicle access through a locked gate on its
private land. See Tr. 94:9-96:3, BLM Exs. 8 and 10.
Upon further investigation BLM concluded that the activities around the
house may have disturbed an archeological resource in violation of ARPA. As a
result, BLM sent a staff archaeologist to the site to record and assess the damage. She
prepared a June 2012 assessment which concluded that the site exhibits
numerous remains of past human life or activities which are of
archaeological in excess of 100 years old, it meets the definition of an
archaeological resource according to the Archaeological Resources Protection Act
(ARPA) as amended (16 U.S.C. 470bb(l))...." BLM Ex. 1 at 3.
She described damage to the archaeological resource caused by the blading of
a road to the west of the house construction. She calculated the total damages to be
$101,540.80. This included the archaeological value of the resource ($98,371.76) plus
the cost of restoration and repair of the site ($3,169.04). Id. at and 11.
BLM then issued Pensco a Notice of Violation ("NOV") (Pensco A),
followed by a Notice of Assessment ("NOA") declaring that Pensco was responsible
for the damage to the archaeological site caused by the unauthorized blading and
house construction. BLM reaffirmed the two components of the proposed penalty of
$101,540.80: $98,371.76 for the archaeological value of the archaeological resource
2
47 OHA 12

ARPA 2013-01
and for the cost of restoration and repair of the site. Pensco subsequently
filed a Request for Hearing regarding the NOA.
BLM filed a motion for summary judgement before the hearing. I denied the
motion because genuine fact issues remained, specifically whether Pensco was
responsible for the blading of the road to the west of the house. In the course of
denying the motion I also ruled in BLM's favor on several alleged deficiencies in
NOV and NOA. Pensco v. BLM, No. ARPA 2013-01 (Dept. of Interior,
Hearings Division, filed Sep. 3, 2013).
I conducted a one day hearing on September 24, 2013 in Shoshone, Idaho. At
the conclusion of testimony the parties declined oral argument in favor of written
submissions and then subsequently stipulated to dispensing with written post-
hearing briefs. Consequently this decision is made without the benefit of argument
from either counsel.
The following sections will address the issues I believe were raised by the
hearing.
III. Analysis
A. Burden and Standard of Proof
Neither ARPA nor its implementing regulations establish the burden and
standard of proof for hearings. But a Department of the Interior appeals board
decision has affirmed an administrative law judge decision that placed the burden
on the Government to prove both the fact of violation and the propriety of the.
penalty assessment by a preponderance of the evidence. In re Harelson, 27 OHA 225,
228 (2004) (citing 5 U.S.C. § 556(d) (2000) and of v. Greenwich Collieries,
512 U.S. 267, 276-78 Accordingly BLM must prove by a preponderance of
This description of the standard and burden of proof differs from that articulated
in two prior administrative law judge decisions. Both of these required that
the [Government] bears the burden of going forward with evidence
sufficient to establish a prima facie case as to the fact of violation and
the propriety of the penalty assessment. If a prima facie case is
presented, the burden then shifts to complainant(s) to overcome [the
Government's] prima facie case.
3
47 OHA 13

ARPA 2013-01
the evidence that Pensco is responsible for the alleged violation and that the penalty
assessment is appropriate.
The Responsibility of Pensco
BLM found that the damage to the archaeological resources had been caused
by blading with heavy equipment on the west side of the house construction site
and that Pensco was responsible. Pensco Ex. A. See Tr. 94:9 - 104:13 - 105:3,
107:19 - 108:23 (testimony of BLM realty specialist). It supported this finding with
evidence that heavy equipment had done the damage, that a person could not easily
access the site with heavy equipment over public land, and that Pensco controlled
the only access for heavy equipment through its private land to the south. Id., Tr.
94:9 - 96:3, 104:13 - 105:3, 107:19 - 108:23 (testimony of BLM realty specialist). See
BLM Exs. 6 and 10. Further Pensco's manager, Mr. Brown, and its trustee, Mr. Saiya,
acknowledged that a contractor hired by Pensco, and Pensco itself, had heavy
equipment on the construction site. Tr. 166:7-24 (Mr. Brown), 188:3—7 (Mr. Saiya).
Pensco, through the testimony of its manager and trustee, expressly denied
that it was responsible for the archaeological damage. They asserted that they had
not bladed the area and had expressly instructed all the contractors' employees not
to use the road on the west side of the house. Mr. Saiya did not want to obstruct the
view from the house and just wanted it to go back to nature. Tr. 155:2—159:1 (Mr.
Brown), Tr. 177:9-180:11 (Mr. Saiya).
I did not find that either Mr. Brown or Mr. Saiya testified credibly. Mr. Brown
testified that he did not remember the name of the excavation contractor on the site.
Tr. 166:11 Yet he remembered the number of its employees he instructed not to
use the west road. Tr. 167:24—168:12. And he remembered the specific instruction he
gave. Tr. find it incredible that he could not remember the name of the
contractor but could remember the instruction and the number of employees he
gave the instruction to. In addition Mr. Brown did not provide the details that one
would expect about such a significant instruction, i.e., when he gave it, where he
gave it, and the other circumstances of his instruction. Consequently I find it more
likely than not that he did not give the instruction at all, or at least not before the
damage occurred.
Eel River Sawmills, Inc. v. United States, Nos. ARPA 90-1 & 90-2, at 3-4 (Dept. of
Interior, Hearings Division, Aug. 10, 1992). Accord Ariz. Silica Sand Co. v. Acting Area
Dir., Bureau of Indian Affairs, No. at 9-10 (Dept of Interior, Hearings
Division, Oct.
4
47 OHA 14

ARPA 2013-01
Mr. Saiya had a better memory about the identity of the excavation
contractor. After first stating that he could not remember the name of the contractor
he identified the contractor as "Petit Construction." Tr. 178:4—18. Then he related
that the contractor started work on its own initiative, without express instructions
from Mr. Saiya, without a written contract, without an agreement on price, and
without written plans. Tr. 182:11-15, 186:4-6, 186:22-187:8. Given these
circumstances, I find it incredible that Mr. Saiya had instructed this contractor not to
use the west road. See 188:10—190:22. Mr. Saiya would have had no need to give
such a specific instruction before the contractor began work at the site because Mr.
Saiya had not even told the contractor to begin. Therefore I find it more likely than
not that Mr. Saiya did not give the instruction at all, or did not give it with the
specificity he related at the hearing. At least Mr. Saiya did not give the instruction
before he learned that the contractor had begun work, thus leaving the possibility
that the damage had already been done before the instruction.
But even if I could accept the testimony of Mr. Brown and Mr. Saiya, Pensco
would still be responsible for the damage. This conclusion requires determining
whether ARPA imposes liability on a party who did not damage the archaeological
site itself and who gave express instructions not to disturb the area where the
damage occurred.
Neither the ARPA statute nor the implementing regulations expressly impose
liability on persons who did not physically damage an archaeological resource. The
statute states:
No person may excavate, remove, damage, or otherwise alter or
deface, or attempt to excavate, remove, damage, or otherwise alter or
deface any archaeological resource located on public lands
16 U.S.C. § 470ee(a). And the content of this statutory section is reiterated in the
regulations at 43 C.F.R. § 7.4(a). But neither of these prohibitions limits liability to
only the person who physically caused the damage.
Where a statute, such as ARPA, does not expressly provide for expanded
liability nor foreclose it, the courts often apply common law principles like,
"vicarious liability," to interpret it. See Mey v. Pinnacle Security, LLC, 2012 WL
4009718 (N.D. W.Va.), at *4 (citing Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280, 285 (2003) ("[W]hen
Congress creates a tort action, it legislates against a legal background of ordinary
tort-related vicarious liability rules and consequently intends its legislation to
5
47 OHA 15

ARPA 2013-01
incorporate those rules.")); BUC Intern Corp. v. International Yacht Council Ltd., 489
F.3d 1139 (11th Cir. 2007) (Where a statute does not specifically provide for
vicarious liability, well established principles derived from common law apply.)
In a situation analogous to ARPA, the courts have held that the Federal Mine
Safety and Health Act of 1977, 30 U.S.C §§ 801-965 (2006) ("MSHA") imposes
responsibility on a mine operator for the violations of another person, even though
the statute did not explicitly provide for it. Like ARPA, MSHA, does not expressly
provide for expanded liability nor does it expressly limit liability to only the person
who physically violated the statute. Nevertheless in Western-Fuels-Utah, Inc. v.
Federal Mine Safety & Health Review 870 F.2d 711 (D.C. Cir. 1989), the court
held a mine operator responsible for the actions of its miner who negligently
violated an MSHA regulation, even though the operator had not been negligent
itself, and could not have foreseen the violation. Id. at 713, 716. The court explained
the underlying common law doctrine:
The general rule of both civil and criminal responsibility is that
a person is not liable for a harm done unless he caused it by his action
(actus reus ), and did so with a certain intent (mens rea ). Strict liability
alters this general rule by eliminating the requirement of mens rea; one
may then be punished for acting in a forbidden way, even if one was
without any particular intent, such as willfulness or negligence. A
familiar example is the strict liability of an enterprise for the
consequences of its ultrahazardous activity, such as the use of
explosives. Vicarious liability, on the other hand, alters the general rule
by holding a person liable for the act of another-that is, by attenuating
the requirement of an actus reus. A familiar example here is the liability
of one coconspirator for the act of another within the scope of the
conspiracy.
Vicarious liability may be imposed with or without regard to
the intent of the actor; in the latter case, which combines strict and
vicarious liability, one person is held liable for an act of another who
was not at fault. An innkeeper, for example, may be liable, both civilly
and criminally, for serving an alcoholic beverage to a minor even if he
has taken action to ensure that minors not be served in his
establishment, was unaware that a minor was being served, and could
not, in the exercise of reasonable care, have stopped the minor from
being served. See W. LaFave and A. Scott, Criminal Law 224-25 (1972).
6
47 OHA 16

ARPA 2013-01
Id. at 713. Prior hearing decisions have held that ARPA establishes a strict liability
standard for civil penalties. Eel River Sawmills, Inc. v. United States, Nos. ARPA 90-1
& 90-2, at (Dept. of Interior, Hearings Division, Aug. 10, Accord Ariz.
Silica Sand Co. v. Acting Area Dir., Bureau of Indian Affairs, No. at 11
(Dept. of Interior, Hearings Division, Oct. 21, 1996).
The evidence shows that either Pensco itself (by Mr. Brown or Mr. Saiya), or
its excavation contractor, must have disturbed the ground on the west side of the
building where BLM found the archaeological damage. Pensco and its contractor
had the heavy equipment capable of doing the damage on site and Pensco controlled
the only roads capable of bringing the heavy equipment to the site. No other actors
have been identified as being at the construction site. Since Mr. Brown, Mr. Saiya,
and the contractor were acting for the benefit of Pensco, it was responsible for their
actions under the doctrine of "vicarious liability."
If the statute were interpreted otherwise, it would allow a person, such as
Pensco, to escape liability for its employees or contractors simply by claiming that
they acted contrary to its instructions. Interpreting the statute to impose vicarious
liability on Pensco promotes the purpose of ARPA - to protect irreplaceable
archaeological resources on public lands. See 46 Fed. Reg. 5566 (Jan.
("[ARPA] has two fundamental purposes: to protect irreplaceable archeological [sic]
resources on public lands . . . ; and to increase communication . . . .").
In this instance the contractor was trespassing on the public lands at the behest of
Pensco and Pensco should bear the ultimate responsibility for the damage to the
archaeological resources.
Having concluded that Pensco is responsible for the damage to the
archaeological resources, attention will now turn to whether BLM properly
calculated the penalty assessment.
The Propriety of the Penalty Assessment
The Government prepared a written Damage Assessment that found a
disturbance of 1,163 cubic yards, covering 7,279 square feet, to an archaeological
resource on public land administered by BLM. It found that the unauthorized
disturbance caused damage to the resources in the total amount of $101,540.80,
consisting of repair and restoration ($3,169.04) and archaeological value ($98,371.76).
BLM Exhibit 1 at BLM assessed a penalty of $101,540.80 equal to the
amount of damages documented in the Damage Assessment.
7
47 OHA 17

ARPA 2013-01
At the hearing BLM introduced a map showing the approximate site
boundaries (BLM Ex. pictures of the disturbed area (BLM Ex. and a map
showing locations of disturbed archaeological artifacts such as flicks and stone tools
(BLM Ex. 7). The BLM archaeologist who prepared the Damage Assessment
testified. And testimony from an Idaho deputy state historic preservation officer (Tr.
112—129) and a Shoshone Bannock tribal cultural resources coordinator (Tr. 129—
135) supported the archaeologist's testimony.
Pensco presented no opposing evidence or argument to counter the damage
assessment evidence. Nevertheless its cross examination appeared to challenge the
archaeologist's measurement of the disturbed area. See BLM Ex. 1 at 10. Pensco
developed evidence that the archaeologist had not actually measured the depth of
the disturbed area. Tr. 38:16-40:3. Rather the witness said she had used a uniform
depth of two inches, which she described as an "educated estimate." Tr. 40:4 - 20.
Further testimony from the state historic preservation officer established that the
BLM archaeologist had "used a conservative estimate as to depth at just five
centimeters, or two inches .. ." Tr. 120:2 - 121:11. After reviewing the testimony I
find that BLM reasonably used an estimate of two inches to calculate the volume of
the disturbed area and that the use of this estimate did not diminish the propriety of
the damage assessment.
Pensco's cross-examination of the archaeologist also attempted to question
the source of the artifacts (Tr. 42:12-44:17, 51:13-52:6), whether cows could have
caused the damage (Tr. 44:18 - 46:13), whether the site met the regulatory definition
of an archaeological resource (Tr.46:14-50:11), and whether the resource had been
actually damaged (Tr. 50:12-51:12, 52:7-53:7). But, effective redirect examination
successfully rehabilitated the witness. Tr. 53:15 - did not find that the cross-
examination undermined the evidence presented by BLM.
Pensco also seems to question whether the site satisfied the required 100-year
age. See Pensco Ex. A at 1 ("exact age of the site could not be determined"). But the
archaeologist opined that that the site was older than 100 years because the artifacts
must have been left before the Shoshone Bannock and Shoshone tribes were
removed to reservation in the Tr. 28:1 — 11.
In summary I conclude that BLM proved, by a preponderance of the
evidence, that its penalty assessment (in an amount equal to the damage to the
archaeological resource) was appropriate.
8
47 OHA 18

ARPA 2013-01
IV. Conclusion
The above analysis has shown that Pensco is responsible under ARPA for the
damage done to archaeological resource on BLM land because ARPA imposes
vicarious liability upon Pensco for the actions of its employees or contractors. And
the evidence has shown that the penalty assessment is appropriate. Therefore I
conclude that BLM has proven, by a preponderance of the evidence, that Pensco is
responsible for the alleged violation and that the penalty assessment is appropriate.
The civil penalty assessed by BLM against Pensco for violation of the
Archaeological Resources Protection Act in the amount of $101,540.80 is affirmed.
Robert G. Holt
Administrative Law Judge
